report:
**Conclusion: No.** The best placebo-controlled evidence does not show that saw palmetto preparations improve urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) over the longer term (about 1 year).

A 2012 Cochrane review (32 randomized trials; 5,666 men) found no improvement versus placebo in symptom scores, nighttime urination, or peak urine flow—including trials using two or three times the usual dose.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001423.pub3/abstract

This is supported by two relatively rigorous, longer trials:

* In a 225-man, double-blind trial lasting one year, standard-dose saw palmetto was not superior to placebo for urinary symptoms or objective BPH measures.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085
* A 72-week placebo-controlled trial tested escalating doses (up to triple standard dose) and likewise found no meaningful symptom benefit.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439

Why might someone think “yes”? An older 1998 systematic review reported possible benefits, but the evidence base then was smaller and included lower-quality, shorter, and heterogeneous studies/extracts.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9820264/?rtkcid=6915dbbcd58b0c71e63f68a4&rtkcmpid=67a65a36b4f47ca0c57e7a46

Different commercial products and combinations (for example, saw palmetto plus other herbs) are not interchangeable, so positive findings for a combination do not establish benefit from saw palmetto itself. Saw palmetto appears generally well tolerated, but it should not replace evaluation of persistent or worsening urinary symptoms.
